passage:
I was in the study group when Sudha said it, so I'll just tell you what I saw.
Our group of four had a project due Monday. On Wednesday Sudha told us the survey analysis was done. On Saturday it turned out she hadn't started. We scrambled for two days.
On Sunday evening she asked us all to stay after the library closed. She didn't sit down.
"I said the analysis was finished. It wasn't. I hadn't even opened the data. I lied because I was embarrassed that I was behind, and I didn't want you to think I was the weak one. Because of that, you lost your weekend. That's on me, not on the deadline or on anyone else."
Nobody said anything. Then she said, "I'm not asking you to be okay with it tonight."
I can't know what she was feeling. Her hands were shaking. But she didn't once say "sorry if".
Thomas

qa.q: On which day did Sudha tell the group the survey analysis was done?
qa.a: Sudha told the group on Wednesday.

qa.q: What does Sudha say she was feeling when she lied?
qa.a: Sudha says she was embarrassed about being behind and did not want the group to think she was the weak one.

qa.q: What made Sudha's apology a full one?
qa.a: She said exactly what she did, why, and what it cost the group, blamed no one else, and did not ask for quick forgiveness.

qa.q: How might the rest of the group feel after the apology?
qa.a: They might still be annoyed about the lost weekend, but hearing the full truth, without excuses, could make it easier to trust Sudha again over time.

grounding: Thomas watches Sudha own a lie to her study group exactly, without excuses or blame, and accept that they may need time.

passage:
Saturday. Santosh told Farida he'd be at the library all evening. He was at the party she had asked him, for a real reason, not to go to that night. She found out from a photo.
Sunday. "Sorry if you felt bad," he texted. "Can we just move on? It's not a big deal." Farida didn't reply. The "if" sat on her screen like a slap.
Tuesday. Santosh reread his message on the bus, face burning. He'd apologised for her feelings, not his lie.
Wednesday. He asked to meet at the college canteen. He didn't reach for her hand.
"On Saturday I said I was at the library. I was at the party. I lied because I didn't want an argument, and that made your reason not matter. That was wrong. My Sunday message made it worse."
Farida looked at him for a long moment.
"I don't expect you to be okay today," he said. "Take the time you need."

qa.q: Where did Santosh say he would be on Saturday evening?
qa.a: Santosh said he would be at the library all evening.

qa.q: How did Farida feel reading "Sorry if you felt bad"?
qa.a: Farida felt hurt again, as if slapped, because the message apologised for her feelings instead of the lie and pushed her to move on.

qa.q: What changed between Santosh's Sunday text and his Wednesday apology?
qa.a: On Wednesday he named exactly what he did and why, admitted his first message made it worse, and did not rush Farida to forgive.

qa.q: What would change if Santosh had stuck with the Sunday message?
qa.a: Farida would likely feel that the lie and the quick brush-off were repeated harm, and the distance between them would grow.

grounding: Over several days, Santosh moves from a vague sorry asking to move on to fully owning what he lied about, without excuses and without rushing Farida.
